foundations-functions.hook: Can a rule have an inverse image without having an inverse function?
foundations-functions.objects: The domain and codomain are part of a function. Write f:X→Y; composition g∘f applies f first. An inverse image is a subset of X, not a reversed arrow.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which rule is a function from {0,1} to {a,b}?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Every input needs exactly one output. Several inputs may share an output; one input may not have two, and an input may not be omitted.

examples.title: An injective map with missing outputs
steps: For f:Z→Z, f(n)=2n, equality 2a=2b forces a=b.
Odd integers have no preimage, so f is not surjective.
The inverse image of {2,3,4} is {1,2}; that set exists even though f has no two-sided inverse.

examples.title: A many-to-one map onto its codomain
steps: For p:Z→{0,1}, let p(n) be the remainder modulo 2.
The fiber of 0 is the even integers and the fiber of 1 is the odd integers.
Both outputs occur, so p is surjective, but p(0)=p(2), so it is not injective.

nonexample.title: Choosing both square roots
nonexample.explanation: The rule x↦±√x from nonnegative real numbers to R assigns two outputs to every positive input. Choosing the nonnegative root gives a function; retaining both roots gives a relation.

proofSteps: If f is bijective, each y∈Y has a unique preimage x∈X. Define h(y)=x.
Uniqueness gives h(f(x))=x; existence gives f(h(y))=y.
Conversely, if hf=id_X and fh=id_Y, then f(x)=f(x′) implies x=hf(x)=hf(x′)=x′.
Every y is f(h(y)), so f is surjective. Both directions are proved.

boundaryCheck.question: For an arbitrary f:X→Y, what does f⁻¹({y}) mean?
choices: All inputs mapped to y, possibly none
boundaryCheck.explanation: Inverse-image notation requires neither injectivity nor surjectivity. Assuming a unique input confuses a fiber with an inverse function.

application.question: For f:{0,1,2,3,4}→{0,1,2}, f(n)=n mod 3, what is f⁻¹({1})?
application.explanation: Both 1 and 4 have remainder 1. A fiber contains every matching input, not just a preferred representative.

transfer.question: Restrict the codomain of n↦2n from Z to 2Z. What changes?
transfer.explanation: The rule and domain stay fixed. Every allowed target now occurs exactly once, so the same rule becomes a bijection Z→2Z. Surjectivity depends on the codomain.

foundations-functions.connection: Fibers turn a function into a partition. Next identify inputs with the same output; quotient maps formalize that identification.

foundations-fibers.hook: Why do equal outputs sort every input into exactly one class?
foundations-fibers.objects: Let f:X→Y be a function. Define x~x′ exactly when f(x)=f(x′). Empty fibers belong to targets outside the image; they are not equivalence classes.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For n↦n mod 3 on {0,1,2,3,4,5}, which inputs share the output of 2?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The fiber includes 2 and 5. A class contains all equivalent inputs, not only its label.

examples.title: Remainder fibers
steps: For f:Z→Z/3Z, the classes are 3Z, 1+3Z and 2+3Z.
Each integer lies in exactly one by division with remainder.
The label 1+3Z names an infinite set; choosing 4 instead gives the same set.

examples.title: A finite partition becomes a function
steps: Partition X={a,b,c,d} into {a,c}, {b}, {d}.
Map each input to its containing block. The codomain is the set of three blocks.
The fibers of this map recover exactly the original partition.

nonexample.title: Nearness is not always equivalence
nonexample.explanation: On Z, define x~y when |x−y|≤1. It is reflexive and symmetric, but 0~1 and 1~2 while 0 is not related to 2. Overlapping neighborhoods do not form equivalence classes.

proofSteps: Reflexivity follows from f(x)=f(x).
Symmetry follows by reversing equality; transitivity follows by chaining equalities.
If two fibers overlap at z, both target values equal f(z), so the fibers coincide. Otherwise they are disjoint.
Every x belongs to its own fiber. Conversely, membership in the same block of a partition is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
The map [x]↦f(x) is well-defined by the defining relation. Equal outputs mean equal classes, so it is injective. Every element of im f has a preimage, so it is surjective onto im f.

boundaryCheck.question: Can two distinct equivalence classes intersect?
choices: No; one shared element forces equality
Only if the set is infinite
boundaryCheck.explanation: Transitivity makes every member of one intersecting class equivalent to every member of the other. Cardinality is irrelevant.

application.question: Which relation on Z is an equivalence relation?
application.explanation: Divisibility of differences is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Strict order fails reflexivity; nearness fails transitivity.

transfer.question: For f:R→R, f(x)=x², describe the quotient by equal outputs.
choices: The classes are {0} and {x,−x} for x>0
There is a separate class for every negative target
transfer.explanation: Positive targets have two opposite preimages; zero has one; negative targets have empty fibers and produce no class. The quotient corresponds to the image [0,∞), not all of R.

foundations-fibers.connection: A quotient collects classes without deleting their members. To define a rule on those classes, the next lesson checks whether outputs survive a change of representative.

foundations-quotient-rules.hook: If a class has many names, how can a formula using one name define a function?
foundations-quotient-rules.objects: Let ~ partition X and ≈ partition Y. A proposed rule F:X/~→Y/≈, [x]↦[f(x)], must send equivalent inputs to equivalent outputs. Equality of output classes, not equality of chosen outputs, is required.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which integers represent the same parity class as 1?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A class includes all equivalent integers, including negative representatives such as −1.

examples.title: A parity swap is well-defined
steps: Define F([n]₂)=[n+1]₂.
If n′=n+2k, then n′+1=(n+1)+2k, so the output parity is unchanged.
The map swaps the even and odd classes and is its own inverse.

examples.title: A rule can depend on both quotient moduli
steps: The rule [n]₄↦[n]₂ works: changing n by a multiple of 4 changes it by a multiple of 2.
Its fibers are pairs of classes modulo 4.
The reverse rule [n]₂↦[n]₄ fails; equal input classes need not yield equal output classes.

nonexample.title: Forgetting brackets changes the question
nonexample.explanation: The proposed map Z/2Z→Z, [n]₂↦n, gives 0 and 2 for the same input class. The integer output has no quotient relation that could identify them.

proofSteps: Necessity: if [x]=[x′], a function must give one output, hence [f(x)]=[f(x′)].
Sufficiency: assume x~x′ implies f(x)≈f(x′). Pick any representative of an input class.
Another representative gives the same output class by assumption, so the output is unambiguous.
This proves well-definedness; injectivity, surjectivity and preservation of operations are separate questions.

boundaryCheck.question: Which equality must be proved for [x]↦[f(x)]?
choices: Every class has only one member
boundaryCheck.explanation: Output representatives may differ while their classes agree. Requiring equality in Y would reject legitimate quotient maps.

application.question: Does [n]₃↦[n²]₆ define a function?
choices: No: 0 and 3 give output classes 0 and 3 modulo 6
application.explanation: 0 and 3 represent the same input; 0² and 3² have different residues modulo 6. One explicit witness disproves well-definedness.

transfer.question: For positive m,n, when is [a]ₘ↦[a]ₙ well-defined?
transfer.explanation: Necessity: 0 and m are equal modulo m, so n must divide m. Sufficiency: every difference divisible by m is then divisible by n. This is a divisibility proof, not a test of a few representatives.

foundations-quotient-rules.connection: Congruence proves that addition and multiplication descend to classes. Normality will solve the same representative problem for products of group cosets.

mh2220-axioms.hook: What do adding integers and composing triangle motions have in common?
mh2220-axioms.objects: A group is a nonempty set G with a function G×G→G. The operation is associative, has a two-sided identity, and every element has a two-sided inverse. Composition applies the right-hand motion first.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Why must a binary operation give exactly one result for each pair?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Functionhood is required before the group axioms. Commutativity and finiteness are not group axioms.

examples.title: Integers under addition
steps: Sums of integers stay in Z, so addition is closed.
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c); zero is a two-sided identity.
The inverse of a is −a. This infinite group is also commutative.

examples.title: Symmetries of a triangle
steps: The six motions preserving an equilateral triangle compose to another such motion.
Composition of functions is associative, the stationary motion is identity, and reversing a motion supplies its inverse.
A rotation and reflection need not commute. Both composition orders must be read right to left.

nonexample.title: Failures must name the axiom
nonexample.explanation: On nonzero integers, addition fails closure since 1+(−1)=0. On Z, subtraction fails associativity: (1−2)−3=−4 but 1−(2−3)=2. Positive integers under addition lack an identity. Nonnegative integers under addition have identity 0 but positive elements lack inverses. A closed multiplication table alone proves none of the remaining axioms.

proofSteps: If e and e′ are both two-sided identities, then e=e·e′=e′.
If b and c are both inverses of a, then b=b·e=b·(a·c)=(b·a)·c=e·c=c.
The middle equality uses associativity. These proofs require neither commutativity nor finiteness.

boundaryCheck.question: A table on a finite set has every output inside the set. What is established?
boundaryCheck.explanation: A table listing outputs establishes closure; associativity compares (ab)c with a(bc) for every triple, and needs a separate argument or exhaustive check.

application.question: Which axiom fails for nonnegative integers under addition?
application.explanation: Zero is an identity and addition is associative and closed, but 1 has no additive inverse inside the nonnegative integers.

transfer.question: In b(ac)=(ba)c when proving uniqueness of inverses, which axiom is used?
transfer.explanation: Associativity changes parentheses without changing order. No swapping of factors is justified in an arbitrary group.

mh2220-axioms.connection: Uniqueness lets us write a⁻¹ without ambiguity. Next reverse a product and distinguish finite order from the size of the whole group.

mh2220-inverse-order.hook: To undo two moves, why must you undo the last move first?
mh2220-inverse-order.objects: Let a,b lie in a group G. Write a⁰=e and a⁻ⁿ=(a⁻¹)ⁿ. The order of a is the least positive n with aⁿ=e, if such n exists; otherwise it is infinite.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which equality uses associativity alone?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Associativity changes grouping; commuting factors is an additional property.

examples.title: Reverse two triangle motions
steps: For rotation r and reflection s, applying rs means s first, then r.
Undo r with r⁻¹, then undo s with s⁻¹=s. The undoing word is sr⁻¹.
Algebraically (rs)(sr⁻¹)=r(ss)r⁻¹=e.

examples.title: Finite and infinite order
steps: In the additive group Z/12Z, successive multiples of 8 are 8,4,0, so 8 has order 3.
In additive Z, the element 1 has infinite order because no positive multiple equals 0.
Order belongs to an element. An infinite group can still have finite-order elements, such as (1 mod 2,0) in C2×Z.

nonexample.title: Power laws can fail across different bases
nonexample.explanation: In S3, let a=(12), b=(23). Then a²b²=e but (ab)² is a nonidentity 3-cycle. Commutativity is sufficient for (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ; it is not a group axiom.

proofSteps: (ab)(b⁻¹a⁻¹)=a(bb⁻¹)a⁻¹=aea⁻¹=e.
(b⁻¹a⁻¹)(ab)=b⁻¹(a⁻¹a)b=b⁻¹eb=e.
Uniqueness of inverse gives (ab)⁻¹=b⁻¹a⁻¹.
If a has finite order n, then (aᵏ)ᵗ=e exactly when n divides kt. Writing d=gcd(n,k), the least positive such t is n/d.
Multiplying ag=bg on the right by g⁻¹ gives a=b. Also (g⁻¹)ᵏ=e iff gᵏ=e, and (hgh⁻¹)ᵏ=hgᵏh⁻¹ by cancellation; these give equality of orders, including infinite order.

boundaryCheck.question: Which assumption guarantees (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ for all positive n?
choices: a and b have the same order
boundaryCheck.explanation: Commutativity lets factors be rearranged. Finiteness or equal orders alone does not.

application.question: If g has order 18, what is the order of g⁶?
application.explanation: The least t with 18 dividing 6t is 3; equivalently 18/gcd(18,6)=3.

transfer.question: If (ab)⁻¹=a⁻¹b⁻¹, what follows about a and b?
transfer.explanation: The inverse formula gives b⁻¹a⁻¹=a⁻¹b⁻¹; invert both sides to obtain ab=ba. This says nothing about other pairs in the group.

mh2220-inverse-order.connection: The powers of one element form a cyclic subgroup. The subgroup test identifies when a more general subset has the same closure properties.

mh2220-subgroups.hook: How can one short test replace three separate group checks?
mh2220-subgroups.objects: A subgroup H≤G uses the inherited operation. The test requires H nonempty and xy⁻¹∈H for every x,y∈H. For additive groups this becomes x−y∈H.

prerequisiteCheck.question: In an additive group, what replaces xy⁻¹?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The inverse operation for addition is negation, so xy⁻¹ in multiplicative notation becomes x+(−y).

examples.title: Even integers
steps: 2Z is nonempty since it contains 0.
For 2a,2b∈2Z, their difference is 2(a−b), which lies in 2Z.
Thus 2Z is a subgroup of additive Z. The same argument works for every nZ, including 0Z={0}.

examples.title: The three rotations inside S3
steps: A3={e,(123),(132)} consists of powers of r=(123).
For rⁱ,rʲ, the product rⁱ(rʲ)⁻¹=rⁱ⁻ʲ is another power of r.
This verifies subgroup closure without treating the triangle picture as a proof.

nonexample.title: Odd integers fail the inherited subgroup test
nonexample.explanation: The difference of two odd integers is even; in particular 1−1=0 is not odd. A nonempty subset is not a subgroup merely because its elements look alike.

proofSteps: Choose h∈H. The test gives hh⁻¹=e∈H, then eh⁻¹=h⁻¹∈H.
For x,y∈H, the inverse y⁻¹ is in H; applying the test to x and y⁻¹ yields xy∈H. Associativity is inherited from G.
For H≤Z, either H={0}, or H contains positive integers (negate a negative member if necessary). Choose the least positive n∈H.
Divide h∈H as h=qn+r, 0≤r<n. Since r=h−qn∈H, minimality forces r=0. Thus H=nZ. Conversely every nZ is a subgroup.
Finally bZ≤aZ exactly when b∈aZ, equivalently a divides b. This includes the zero subgroup: 0Z≤aZ for every a.

boundaryCheck.question: Why must the subgroup test require nonemptiness?
choices: Otherwise the empty set passes the universal test vacuously
boundaryCheck.explanation: The empty set satisfies every universally quantified closure condition but has no identity. Nonemptiness rules out that false positive.

application.question: Which inclusion is true?
application.explanation: Every multiple of 6 is even, but 2 is not a multiple of 6. Larger divisors give smaller subgroups.

transfer.question: A subgroup of Z contains 12 and 18. What must it contain?
transfer.explanation: It contains 18−12=6 and all multiples of 6. It need not contain 1: 6Z itself is a counterexample.

mh2220-subgroups.connection: Intersections preserve subgroup conditions; unions generally do not. Generated subgroups supply the smallest subgroup containing a chosen set.

mh2220-generators.hook: If a union of subgroups fails, what is the smallest repair?
mh2220-generators.objects: For S⊆G, ⟨S⟩ is the intersection of all subgroups containing S, equivalently all finite words in S and inverses. The join H∨K is ⟨H∪K⟩, not usually H∪K.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which closure operation must a subgroup of additive Z allow?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A subgroup contains inverses and sums, hence differences. Restricting to positive combinations generally gives a monoid instead.

examples.title: Two integer generators
steps: Euclid gives 18=1·12+6 and 12=2·6.
Back-substitute: 6=18−12. Every integer combination of 12 and 18 is a multiple of 6, and every multiple of 6 is such a combination.
Therefore ⟨12,18⟩=6Z. This is the Bézout mechanism, not a statement that 12Z∪18Z already contains every multiple of 6.

examples.title: Two transpositions generate S3
steps: Let a=(12) and b=(23). Their products give ab=(123), ba=(132), and aba=(13).
Together with e,a,b these are all six permutations of three letters.
Thus ⟨a,b⟩=S3, while ⟨a⟩∪⟨b⟩ has only e,a,b and omits ab.

nonexample.title: Relations need a completeness argument
nonexample.explanation: If a,b satisfy a²=b²=(ab)³=e in a group, this only defines a homomorphism from the presented group onto ⟨a,b⟩. To claim an isomorphism, show no additional relations collapse it; for S3 one can combine a six-word upper bound with six distinct images.

proofSteps: Every subgroup containing S contains every word in S and inverse letters.
The set of all such words contains e, is closed under concatenation, and is closed under reversing and inverting a word. Thus it is a subgroup.
These two inclusions identify it with the intersection definition.
For integer generators a,b, every common divisor divides all combinations; the Euclidean algorithm expresses gcd(a,b) as a combination. Hence ⟨a,b⟩=gcd(a,b)Z.

For the presentation a²=b²=(ab)³=e, cancel adjacent aa or bb. The relation gives abab=ba, baba=ab and aba=bab, so every alternating word reduces to one of e,a,b,ab,ba,aba. These six words have distinct images under a=(12), b=(23), proving that this presentation gives S3 rather than a smaller quotient.

boundaryCheck.question: Does a list of relations automatically prove a proposed presentation is complete?
choices: No; one must rule out extra relations
boundaryCheck.explanation: Relations establish a quotient map. Surjectivity from generating is not injectivity; a normal-form or order argument is needed.

application.question: What is 4Z∨6Z in the subgroup lattice of Z?
application.explanation: Since 2=6−4, the join contains 2Z. Both original subgroups lie in 2Z, proving equality. The intersection, not the join, is 12Z.

transfer.question: Why is H∪K a subgroup exactly when one subgroup contains the other?
choices: Choose h∈H\K and k∈K\H; hk can belong to neither if the union is closed
It depends only on their orders
transfer.explanation: If hk∈H, then k=h⁻¹(hk)∈H, contradiction. If hk∈K, then h=(hk)k⁻¹∈K, contradiction. If one subgroup contains the other, the union is that subgroup.

mh2220-generators.connection: One-generator subgroups are cyclic. Their exponent arithmetic turns generation, order and inclusion into divisibility.

mh2220-congruence.hook: Why is arithmetic on residue classes independent of the chosen integers?
mh2220-congruence.objects: Fix n≥1. Define a≡b mod n when n divides a−b. The class [a] is a+nZ on the integer line. Addition gives an abelian group; adding multiplication gives the ring Z/nZ.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which representatives belong to [2] modulo 5?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Representatives differ by multiples of the modulus; they need not have the same parity.

examples.title: Changing both addends
steps: Use representatives 7 and −1 instead: 7+(−1)=6, still [1].
In general (a+kn)+(b+ℓn)−(a+b)=(k+ℓ)n.

examples.title: Changing both factors
steps: Use 7 and −1: their product is −7, whose class is also [3].
The product difference is (a+kn)(b+ℓn)−ab=n(kb+ℓa+kℓn), a multiple of n.

nonexample.title: Dividing by a class is not always allowed
nonexample.explanation: Modulo 6, [2][1]=[2][4] but [1]≠[4]. Cancellation by [2] fails because [2] is not a unit. Well-defined multiplication does not make every nonzero class invertible.

proofSteps: Reflexivity: n divides a−a=0. Symmetry: if n divides a−b, it divides b−a.
Transitivity: if n divides a−b and b−c, it divides their sum a−c.
Changing representatives in a sum changes it by a multiple of n, so addition is well-defined.
The displayed product expansion proves multiplication is well-defined. Identity, inverses for addition, and distributivity descend from Z.
Division with remainder supplies exactly n distinct classes [0],…,[n−1]. Every [k] is k copies of [1] under addition, proving that the additive group is cyclic of order n.

boundaryCheck.question: What must be checked to define multiplication of classes?
choices: The product is independent of both representatives
boundaryCheck.explanation: Independence is the quotient-rule condition. Invertibility is a separate property and fails in many residue rings.

application.question: Modulo 7, what is [−3][5]?
application.explanation: −15 differs from 6 by −21, a multiple of 7. Representatives need not lie in the standard range.

transfer.question: Why is (a+kn)(b+ℓn) equivalent to ab modulo n?
choices: Because both factors are equal as integers
transfer.explanation: Factoring n from the difference proves independence for every positive modulus. Primality is unnecessary.

mh2220-congruence.connection: This is the first complete quotient construction. Coset multiplication repeats the same proof obligation in a group where factors may not commute.

mh2220-cyclic.hook: How much of a group can one element generate?
mh2220-cyclic.objects: Write ⟨g⟩={gᵏ:k∈Z}. Infinite cyclic groups use integer exponents uniquely; a finite cyclic group of order n identifies exponents modulo n.

prerequisiteCheck.question: If g has order 12, when is gᵃ=gᵇ?
choices: When a and b are positive
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Multiply by g⁻ᵇ. Equality is equivalent to gᵃ⁻ᵇ=e, so the order divides the exponent difference.

examples.title: Every subgroup of C12
steps: For d=1,2,3,4,6,12, the subgroup ⟨gᵈ⟩ has order 12/d.
These are all subgroups: C12, ⟨g²⟩, ⟨g³⟩, ⟨g⁴⟩, ⟨g⁶⟩ and {e}.

examples.title: Infinite cyclic structure
steps: The group ⟨1⟩ under addition is Z: distinct integer exponents give distinct elements.
Its subgroups are dZ for d≥0, by the least-positive-element argument.
There is no finite return time for 1, so reducing all exponents modulo a fixed positive n would collapse distinct elements.

nonexample.title: Equal order does not force cyclicity
nonexample.explanation: C2×C2 has order 4 but every nonidentity element has order 2. No element can generate all four elements, unlike C4.

proofSteps: If no positive power of g is e, equality gᵃ=gᵇ forces a=b; the exponent map Z→⟨g⟩ is a bijective homomorphism.
Otherwise choose the least positive return n. Division by n shows each exponent has the same power as its remainder, and the n remainders give distinct powers.
For H≤⟨g⟩, the exponent set {k:gᵏ∈H} is a subgroup of Z, say dZ. In the finite case it contains nZ, so d divides n.
Thus H=⟨gᵈ⟩ and has n/d elements. The condition (gᵏ)ᵗ=e is n|kt, giving order n/gcd(n,k) and one subgroup for each divisor order.

boundaryCheck.question: Does every finite group have a subgroup for every divisor of its order?
choices: Not in general; the cyclic hypothesis gives this conclusion
boundaryCheck.explanation: Lagrange is a necessary divisibility statement. The existence and uniqueness for every divisor here uses cyclic structure.

application.question: Which elements generate C12?
application.explanation: A power generates exactly when its exponent is coprime to 12.

transfer.question: In C12, which subgroup has order 4 and why is it unique?
choices: ⟨g⁴⟩, because the exponent equals the order
⟨g³⟩, because its exponent subgroup must be 3Z
Any subgroup generated by a nonidentity element
transfer.explanation: The subgroup order is 12/d, so d=3. The classification by exponent subgroups proves uniqueness, not merely one example.

mh2220-cyclic.connection: Cosets compare an arbitrary subgroup with its ambient group; cyclic exponent arithmetic supplies the recurring concrete model.

mh2220-cosets.hook: When do two different representatives name exactly the same subset?
mh2220-cosets.objects: For H≤G, a left coset is gH={gh:h∈H}; a right coset is Hg. Products of permutations apply the right-hand permutation first. A coset need not be a subgroup.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For H=3Z in additive Z, which elements are in 1+H?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A coset translates every element of H. It is a whole set, not a pair of labels.

examples.title: The three left cosets of an order-two subgroup
steps: In S3 take H={e,(12)} and r=(123).
The left cosets are H, rH={(123),(13)}, and r²H={(132),(23)}. These three disjoint pairs contain all six elements.
The right coset Hr={(123),(23)} differs from rH, so left and right cosets need not agree.

examples.title: Residue classes as additive cosets
steps: In Z take H=4Z. The four cosets are 4Z,1+4Z,2+4Z,3+4Z.
The representatives 1 and 9 give the same coset because 9−1∈4Z.
Each coset is in bijection with 4Z by translation, although all are infinite.

nonexample.title: Cosets are not conjugacy classes
nonexample.explanation: The conjugacy class of (12) in S3 contains all three transpositions. The coset H={e,(12)} contains identity and one transposition. Conjugation and translation construct different sets.

proofSteps: If aH=bH, then a=bh for some h∈H, hence b⁻¹a∈H.
If b⁻¹a∈H, write a=bh; then aH=bhH=bH.
If aH and bH intersect at x=ah=bk, then b⁻¹a=kh⁻¹∈H, so the cosets coincide. Thus they are equal or disjoint.
The map H→aH, h↦ah, is bijective with inverse x↦a⁻¹x. This proves equal sizes, without assuming G finite.

boundaryCheck.question: What is the left-coset equality test?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Every coset has the same size; equal size does not imply equal subsets. The order of multiplication in the membership test matters.

application.question: For H={e,(12)} in S3, which coset contains (13)?
application.explanation: (123)(12)=(13), so (13) belongs to (123)H. Read the composition right to left.

transfer.question: A subgroup H of a possibly infinite G has a coset aH. Why are their cardinalities equal?
choices: All subsets of G have equal size
Lagrange applies only to finite G, so there is no argument
transfer.explanation: The explicit bijection works for finite and infinite groups. Finite counting is a later consequence.

mh2220-cosets.connection: A partition into equally sized cosets proves Lagrange. To multiply the classes, however, we must first test normality.

mh2220-lagrange.hook: Why must a subgroup order divide the group order—and why is the converse false?
mh2220-lagrange.objects: Let G be finite and H≤G. The index [G:H] counts left cosets. The same bijection used for cosets gives |G|=[G:H]|H|.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Why do cosets partition a group?
choices: They are equal or disjoint and every element lies in its own coset
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Only the coset H contains identity. Equal-or-disjoint plus coverage gives the partition.

examples.title: Counting S3 by pairs
steps: For H={e,(12)}, the cosets H,(123)H,(132)H are three disjoint pairs.
Translation gives two elements in each pair.
Thus 6=3·2, and [S3:H]=3.

examples.title: An element order is a subgroup order
steps: In C12, g⁴ generates {e,g⁴,g⁸}, a subgroup of order 3.
Its four cosets partition the twelve elements, so 12=4·3.
For any element a of a finite G, applying Lagrange to ⟨a⟩ shows ord(a) divides |G|.

nonexample.title: A4 has no subgroup of order 6
nonexample.explanation: Suppose H had order 6 in A4. Its index would be two, so left and right cosets are H and its complement; hence H is normal. The quotient map to a group of order two sends every 3-cycle to identity, since its image has order dividing both 3 and 2. Then H contains identity and all eight 3-cycles, at least nine elements—a contradiction.

proofSteps: Choose one representative from each left coset. The cosets cover G and are pairwise disjoint.
For each representative a, h↦ah is a bijection H→aH, so each coset has |H| elements.
Adding the sizes of the [G:H] cosets gives |G|=[G:H]|H|.
Divisibility follows from this product. Nothing in the proof constructs a subgroup of a prescribed divisor order.
Let d=ord(g). Since d divides |G|, write |G|=kd to obtain g^|G|=(gᵈ)ᵏ=e. If |G|=p is prime, choose g≠e; its order divides p and exceeds 1, hence is p, so G=⟨g⟩≅Cp.

boundaryCheck.question: What extra hypothesis makes this an integer divisibility statement?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Coset bijections do not require finiteness, but the finite product of integer orders does. Neither normality nor commutativity is used.

application.question: If |G|=60 and |H|=12, how many left cosets are there?
application.explanation: The cosets partition G into pieces of size 12, so the index is 60/12=5.

transfer.question: Why does 6 dividing 12 not guarantee a subgroup of order 6 in A4?
choices: Divisibility is necessary, not sufficient; the index-two argument contradicts existence
Only prime group orders satisfy Lagrange
transfer.explanation: A4 supplies a concrete counterexample to the converse while satisfying Lagrange for every subgroup it actually has.

mh2220-lagrange.connection: Cauchy and Sylow give existence results beyond Lagrange. Normality explains when a coset partition also carries a group operation.

mh2220-homomorphism.hook: How much structure can a map preserve while identifying different inputs?
mh2220-homomorphism.objects: A group homomorphism φ:G→K satisfies φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b). Its image is a subgroup of K; its kernel is the fiber of e_K. Images of a fixed nonempty fiber are described by a coset of the kernel.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Is the image of a function always its whole codomain?
choices: No; it consists of outputs actually attained
Only if the domain is finite
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Surjectivity is the claim that image equals codomain; it is not built into the word function.

examples.title: Reduction modulo six
steps: For φ:Z→Z/6Z, φ(n)=[n], we have φ(a+b)=[a+b]=[a]+[b].
Its kernel is 6Z and its image is all of Z/6Z.
The fiber over [2] is 2+6Z.

examples.title: A homomorphism that misses targets
steps: Let i:2Z→Z be inclusion, using addition on both groups. It preserves sums.
The kernel is {0}, so it is injective. Its image is 2Z, not its codomain Z.
An odd target has an empty fiber; the fiber over 4 is {4}.

nonexample.title: Preserving a set is not preserving its law
nonexample.explanation: The map f:Z→Z, f(n)=n+1, is bijective but not an additive homomorphism: f(0)=1≠0 and f(1+1)=3 while f(1)+f(1)=4.

proofSteps: φ(e)=φ(e)φ(e); multiply by φ(e)⁻¹ to obtain φ(e)=e.
φ(g)φ(g⁻¹)=φ(gg⁻¹)=e, so φ(g⁻¹)=φ(g)⁻¹.
If φ(x)=φ(g), then φ(g⁻¹x)=e, hence x∈g ker φ. Conversely x=gk with k∈ker φ gives φ(x)=φ(g).
Thus each nonempty fiber is g ker φ; empty fibers are precisely the targets outside im φ.
The image is a subgroup: φ(a)φ(b)⁻¹=φ(ab⁻¹) is in the image, which contains identity. For n∈ker φ, φ(gng⁻¹)=φ(g)eφ(g)⁻¹=e; inverse conjugation gives equality of the kernel with its conjugate.

boundaryCheck.question: Which conclusion holds for every homomorphism φ:G→K?
choices: G/ker φ is isomorphic to K
Every nonempty fiber is a coset of ker φ
boundaryCheck.explanation: The image can be smaller than K. The quotient theorem targets im φ unless surjectivity is separately established.

application.question: For φ:Z→Z/6Z, φ(n)=[2n], what are kernel and image?
application.explanation: 6 divides 2n exactly when 3 divides n. The attainable classes are the even residues.

transfer.question: A homomorphism has trivial kernel. What can you conclude without extra hypotheses?
choices: It is injective but may not be surjective
transfer.explanation: Equal outputs give g⁻¹h in the kernel, hence g=h. Inclusion 2Z→Z shows surjectivity need not follow.

mh2220-homomorphism.connection: Kernels provide normal subgroups automatically. Quotienting by a kernel turns the map into an isomorphism onto its actual image.

mh2220-isomorphism.hook: When does a change of names preserve the whole group?
mh2220-isomorphism.objects: An isomorphism φ:G→K is a bijective homomorphism. Check law preservation, injectivity and surjectivity separately. Groups with different element orders cannot be isomorphic.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which condition is missing if a homomorphism is injective?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: An injective homomorphism may embed a proper subgroup into a larger group. An isomorphism must reach the entire codomain.

examples.title: Integers and even integers
steps: Define φ:Z→2Z by φ(n)=2n.
It preserves addition; 2a=2b implies a=b; every target 2k is φ(k).
The inverse ψ:2Z→Z sends 2k to k. The groups are isomorphic despite being different subsets.

examples.title: A finite isomorphism from powers
steps: Let r be a rotation of a triangle through 120°. Define φ:Z/3Z→⟨r⟩ by [k]↦rᵏ.
If k changes by 3m, rᵏ is unchanged. Products correspond to addition of exponents.
The three powers e,r,r² are distinct and exhaustive, proving injectivity and surjectivity.

nonexample.title: Equal size is too weak
nonexample.explanation: C4 and C2×C2 both have four elements. C4 has an element of order four, while every nonidentity element of C2×C2 has order two. No isomorphism can exist. Matching a few invariants, conversely, does not by itself prove isomorphism.

proofSteps: Let φ be a bijective homomorphism and write u=φ(a), v=φ(b); surjectivity permits these choices.
Then φ⁻¹(uv)=φ⁻¹(φ(a)φ(b))=φ⁻¹(φ(ab))=ab=φ⁻¹(u)φ⁻¹(v).
Thus the inverse is a homomorphism. If φ(g)ᵐ=e, then φ(gᵐ)=e; injectivity implies gᵐ=e, so element orders are preserved in both directions.

boundaryCheck.question: Two finite groups have the same order and the same number of generators. Is an isomorphism proved?
choices: No; an explicit structure-preserving bijection or a sufficient theorem is still needed
boundaryCheck.explanation: Matching invariants is useful evidence, but it is not a construction or proof of a bijective homomorphism.

application.question: Which map is an additive isomorphism Z→3Z?
application.explanation: Multiplication by 3 preserves sums, is injective, and reaches every multiple of 3. Translation does not preserve identity; squaring does not preserve sums.

transfer.question: Why may the proof that φ⁻¹ preserves products write u=φ(a) and v=φ(b)?
transfer.explanation: Surjectivity supplies preimages of arbitrary codomain elements; injectivity later makes the inverse a function.

mh2220-isomorphism.connection: The first isomorphism theorem constructs a structure-preserving bijection from any homomorphism, after its kernel has been identified.

mh2220-normal.hook: Does preserving a subgroup under conjugation mean fixing each of its elements?
mh2220-normal.objects: N◁G means gNg⁻¹=N as sets for every g∈G. It is equivalent to gN=Ng. Centrality is stronger: every n∈N commutes individually with every g∈G.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is g(12)g⁻¹ when g=(123)?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Conjugation relabels a transposition: (g(1) g(2))=(23).

examples.title: Normal but not central
steps: A3={e,(123),(132)} is the kernel of sign:S3→{±1}, so it is normal.
Conjugation by (12) swaps (123) with (132).
The subgroup is preserved as a set while its elements move; A3 is not central in S3.

examples.title: Every subgroup of an abelian group
steps: If G is abelian, gng⁻¹=n for every n∈N≤G.
Therefore every subgroup N is normal.
For example 3Z is normal in additive Z; left and right cosets are both translates.

nonexample.title: A transposition subgroup moves
nonexample.explanation: H={e,(12)} in S3 is not normal: conjugating by (123) gives {e,(23)}, a different subgroup. Equal subgroup orders do not make the subgroups equal.

proofSteps: If gNg⁻¹=N, multiply the set equality on the right by g to obtain gN=Ng. Conversely multiply gN=Ng by g⁻¹.
For a homomorphism φ and n∈ker φ, φ(gng⁻¹)=φ(g)eφ(g)⁻¹=e, so gNg⁻¹⊆N.
Apply the same argument to g⁻¹ for the reverse inclusion. Thus every kernel is normal.
For index two, the only cosets are N and its complement, on both left and right, so N is normal. The sign homomorphism has kernel An, hence An◁Sn; for n=1 the same kernel statement remains valid.

boundaryCheck.question: Normality requires which condition?
choices: Every conjugation preserves N as a set
Every element of N is fixed by every conjugation
N has the same order as each of its conjugates
boundaryCheck.explanation: Setwise preservation is the condition. Pointwise fixation is centrality; equal order holds for all conjugate subgroups and is insufficient.

application.question: Which is normal but not central in S3?
application.explanation: A3 is a kernel but a transposition conjugates its two nonidentity elements into each other.

transfer.question: A subgroup H has index two. Why is it normal?
choices: Its two left and two right cosets are H and G\H
Its elements all have order two
transfer.explanation: Any coset other than H is its complement. Thus left and right cosets agree for each representative, giving normality without centrality.

mh2220-normal.connection: Normality is exactly the condition that lets the coset partition inherit representative multiplication.

mh2220-quotient.hook: Why does a coset space sometimes refuse to be a group?
mh2220-quotient.objects: For N◁G, G/N is the set of cosets, with (aN)(bN)=abN. One element of G/N is a whole subset of G. Quotienting identifies elements; it does not remove N from the set.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is one element of G/N?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Cosets are the new elements. The subgroup N itself becomes the identity coset.

examples.title: Parity as a group quotient
steps: For G=Z and N=2Z, the quotient has two elements: the even and odd cosets.
Odd plus odd is even, even plus odd is odd, and 2Z is identity.
Every integer remains represented inside a coset; none is deleted.

examples.title: The quotient S3/A3
steps: A3 consists of even permutations; its other coset consists of the three transpositions.
Products of two odd permutations are even, so the quotient multiplication matches C2.
All six original permutations are grouped into two new elements of size three.

nonexample.title: Two representatives give incompatible products
nonexample.explanation: Let H={e,s}≤S3 with s=(12), and t=(23). The identity class H can be represented by e or s. Multiplying H by tH using e gives tH={(23),(132)}. Using s gives stH={(123),(13)}. These are different cosets, so the proposed multiplication is not well-defined.

proofSteps: Suppose a′=an and b′=bm with n,m∈N. Then a′b′=anbm=ab(b⁻¹nb)m.
Normality gives b⁻¹nb∈N, so a′b′N=abN. This checks both representatives.
Associativity descends from G. Identity is N and the inverse of aN is a⁻¹N.
Conversely, if representative multiplication is well-defined, replacing e by n∈N in N·bN gives nbN=bN, hence b⁻¹nb∈N. Applying inverse conjugation gives normality.
The natural map π(g)=gN preserves products by the quotient law and reaches every coset. Its kernel consists of g with gN=N, precisely N. For finite G, Lagrange gives |G/N|=|G|/|N|.

boundaryCheck.question: Which factor in the well-definedness calculation must lie in N?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Normality moves n past b: anbm=ab(b⁻¹nb)m. Closure alone would not place the conjugate in N.

application.question: What is the identity of Z/5Z?
application.explanation: The zero coset is the identity for addition. It contains all multiples of 5, including 0.

transfer.question: H≤G is not normal. What still exists?
choices: The set of left cosets, but not representative multiplication as a quotient group
A quotient group with identity omitted
transfer.explanation: Cosets and their partition exist for every subgroup. Normality adds a well-defined quotient group law.

mh2220-quotient.connection: The natural projection G→G/N is a surjective homomorphism with kernel N. The first isomorphism theorem reverses this construction.

mh2220-first-isomorphism.hook: After identifying equal outputs, what information does a homomorphism retain?
mh2220-first-isomorphism.objects: For φ:G→K, put N=ker φ. The induced map φ̄:G/N→im φ sends gN to φ(g). The factorization is G→G/N→im φ↪K. The final inclusion need not be surjective.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For φ:Z→Z/6Z, φ(n)=[2n], what is ker φ?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: 2n is divisible by 6 exactly when n is divisible by 3.

examples.title: Reduction onto six classes
steps: For φ(n)=[n] in Z/6Z, the kernel is 6Z and every class is attained.
The induced map Z/6Z→Z/6Z sends n+6Z to [n].
It gives the familiar quotient interpretation without changing the codomain.

examples.title: A genuinely non-surjective map
steps: For φ:Z→Z/6Z, φ(n)=[2n], the kernel is 3Z.
The image is {[0],[2],[4]}, a subgroup of order 3.
The induced isomorphism Z/3Z→{[0],[2],[4]} sends [n]₃ to [2n]₆. It cannot be an isomorphism onto all six classes.

nonexample.title: The codomain cannot replace the image
nonexample.explanation: The inclusion 2Z→Z has trivial kernel. Its quotient by the kernel is 2Z and the induced map reaches only 2Z inside Z. Although these abstract groups happen to be isomorphic by another map, the inclusion is not onto Z.

proofSteps: Well-definedness: if gN=hN, then h⁻¹g∈N, so φ(h)⁻¹φ(g)=e and φ(g)=φ(h).
Homomorphism: φ̄((gN)(hN))=φ(gh)=φ(g)φ(h).
Injectivity: if φ̄(gN)=φ̄(hN), then h⁻¹g∈ker φ=N, hence gN=hN.
Surjectivity onto the image: every y∈im φ equals φ(g) for some g, so y=φ̄(gN). No larger target is claimed.

boundaryCheck.question: When may the theorem conclude G/ker φ≅K for this induced map?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Surjectivity is exactly im φ=K. Injectivity controls the kernel instead.

application.question: For n↦[2n]₆, which quotient models the image?
application.explanation: The kernel is 3Z, so the quotient has three classes corresponding to the three attainable outputs.

transfer.question: Equal induced outputs imply h⁻¹g∈ker φ. Which part of the proof does this establish?
transfer.explanation: It turns equal outputs into equal input cosets. Surjectivity instead starts from an arbitrary element of the image and finds a preimage.

mh2220-first-isomorphism.connection: The second and third isomorphism theorems are applications of this four-step mechanism to carefully chosen restriction and projection maps.

mh2220-second-isomorphism.hook: What does a subgroup look like after a normal subgroup has been collapsed?
mh2220-second-isomorphism.objects: Let H≤G and N◁G. Then HN≤G, N◁HN, H∩N◁H, and H/(H∩N)≅HN/N via h(H∩N)↦hN.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which map suggests the kernel H∩N?
choices: The set inclusion N→H without hypotheses
The map h↦h⁻¹ for any group
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Restrict the quotient projection to H; precisely the elements of H lying in N go to the identity coset.

examples.title: A nontrivial intersection in C12
steps: Write C12 additively; take H=⟨2⟩={0,2,4,6,8,10} and N=⟨3⟩={0,3,6,9}.
H∩N={0,6} has order 2; H+N=C12 since 3−2=1.
H/(H∩N) and C12/N both have order 3. The isomorphism sends h+{0,6} to h+N.

examples.title: A transposition subgroup inside S3
steps: Take H={e,(12)} and N=A3. Their intersection is {e} and HN=S3.
The restriction of sign to H is bijective onto {±1}.
The theorem identifies H/{e} with S3/A3, both of order 2.

nonexample.title: Subgroup products need not be subgroups without normality
nonexample.explanation: In S3, take H={e,(12)} and K={e,(23)}. Their product HK has four elements. It cannot be a subgroup of a group of order six by Lagrange. The hypothesis N◁G is doing real work.

proofSteps: For h₁n₁,h₂n₂∈HN, their product is h₁h₂(h₂⁻¹n₁h₂)n₂∈HN; normality places the conjugate in N. Inverses similarly lie in HN.
N remains normal in HN. Restrict the quotient projection to H: q(h)=hN.
Its image is all HN/N because hnN=hN, and its kernel is H∩N, which is therefore normal in H.
Apply the first isomorphism theorem. The induced rule h(H∩N)↦hN inherits well-definedness and bijectivity from it.

boundaryCheck.question: Why is H∩N normal in H?
choices: It is the kernel of the restricted quotient map
Every intersection is normal in G
boundaryCheck.explanation: The kernel argument works without H being abelian or normal in G.

application.question: In the C12 example, what is |H/(H∩N)|?
application.explanation: |H|=6 and |H∩N|=2, so the quotient has order 3.

transfer.question: A coset hnN in HN/N is represented by which element of H?
transfer.explanation: Since n∈N, hnN=hN. This establishes surjectivity of the restriction onto HN/N even when hn is not in H.

mh2220-second-isomorphism.connection: A restriction produces the second theorem. A projection between two nested quotients produces the third.

mh2220-third-isomorphism.hook: Does collapsing in two stages give the same result as collapsing at once?
mh2220-third-isomorphism.objects: Let N≤M≤G with both N and M normal in G. The map G/N→G/M sends gN to gM. Its kernel is M/N; therefore (G/N)/(M/N)≅G/M.

prerequisiteCheck.question: When does aN=bN imply aM=bM?
choices: Whenever N and M have equal size
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: aN=bN gives b⁻¹a∈N⊆M. Containment supplies representative independence.

examples.title: Two-stage quotient of C12
steps: In additive C12, let N={0,6} and M={0,3,6,9}.
G/N has six elements and M/N has two. Quotienting again gives three elements.
Directly G/M also has three elements; (g+N)+(M/N) maps to g+M.

examples.title: Integer quotients
steps: In Z, take N=12Z and M=3Z. The containment is 12Z≤3Z.
The first quotient is Z/12Z; M/N={0,3,6,9} modulo 12.
The final quotient identifies residues differing by 3, producing Z/3Z.

nonexample.title: Reversed containment breaks the rule
nonexample.explanation: A rule gN↦gM need not be well-defined if N is not contained in M. With N=2Z and M=4Z, 0 and 2 name the same input class but different output classes.

proofSteps: Well-definedness: gN=hN implies h⁻¹g∈N≤M, hence gM=hM.
The map respects products and is surjective because every gM has preimage gN.
Its kernel consists of gN with g∈M, exactly M/N. Thus M/N is normal in G/N.
Apply the first isomorphism theorem to get the induced bijection (gN)(M/N)↦gM. A class of classes corresponds to one larger coset.

boundaryCheck.question: Which normality assumptions make both displayed quotient groups valid?
boundaryCheck.explanation: N◁G is needed for G/N; M◁G for G/M. Merely being normal in M does not suffice.

application.question: If |G|=24, |N|=2 and |M|=8 with the stated hypotheses, what is |(G/N)/(M/N)|?
application.explanation: |G/N|=12 and |M/N|=4; the quotient has 12/4=3 elements, agreeing with |G/M|.

transfer.question: What is one element of (G/N)/(M/N)?
choices: A coset of M/N in G/N, consisting of N-cosets
A chosen element of M only
transfer.explanation: The two-stage quotient has classes of classes. The theorem identifies that collection with a single coset of M in G.

mh2220-third-isomorphism.connection: Correspondence organizes every subgroup between N and G, making nested quotient constructions visible in one lattice interval.

mh2220-correspondence.hook: Which part of a subgroup lattice survives a quotient?
mh2220-correspondence.objects: Let q:G→G/N be the projection with N◁G. Subgroups H with N≤H≤G correspond to subgroups K≤G/N by H↦H/N and K↦q⁻¹(K).

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is q⁻¹(K) for a subgroup K of G/N?
choices: An inverse function, which cannot exist
One chosen representative from each coset
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: An inverse image is a full subset, not an inverse function or a section choosing representatives.

examples.title: The interval above a kernel in C12
steps: Take N=⟨g⁴⟩ of order 3 in C12. Subgroups containing N have orders 3,6,12.
They are N, ⟨g²⟩ and C12; their quotient subgroups have orders 1,2,4 in C12/N≅C4.
The subgroup ⟨g³⟩ of order 4 does not contain N, so it is outside the correspondence interval.

examples.title: A quotient with only two subgroups
steps: Take S3→S3/A3≅C2. Subgroups above A3 are A3 and S3.
They correspond to the identity subgroup and all of C2.
A transposition subgroup has image C2 too, but it is not in the interval above A3 and cannot be recovered by taking the full inverse image.

nonexample.title: Images forget subgroups below the kernel interval
nonexample.explanation: For H={e,(12)}≤S3, q(H)=C2 under the sign quotient. Its full preimage is S3, not H. In general q⁻¹(q(H))=HN, so recovering H requires N≤H.

proofSteps: Inverse images of subgroups under a homomorphism are subgroups and contain its kernel. Images of subgroups are subgroups.
If N≤H, then gN∈H/N exactly when g∈H, so q⁻¹(H/N)=H.
For K≤G/N, surjectivity of q gives q(q⁻¹(K))=K. Thus the two operations are inverse.
Both operations preserve inclusion. Normality corresponds because q(g)q(h)q(g)⁻¹=q(ghg⁻¹); surjectivity tests every conjugator in G/N.

For N≤K≤H, the map of coset sets hK↦(hN)(K/N) is bijective by the same representative test. Therefore [H:K]=[H/N:K/N], even when K is not normal; these are indices of subgroups, not asserted quotient groups.

boundaryCheck.question: Which subgroups of G participate bijectively?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Without N≤H, inverse image after image returns HN, which may be larger than H.

application.question: For C12/N≅C4 with |N|=3, which subgroup order upstairs corresponds to order 2 downstairs?
application.explanation: The subgroup upstairs consists of two cosets, each of size |N|=3, so it has order 6.

transfer.question: For H≤G, why is q⁻¹(q(H))=HN?
choices: gN=hN for some h∈H exactly when g=hn for n∈N
Because inverse images choose one representative
transfer.explanation: Equality of cosets is the membership argument. It explains precisely what information the quotient forgets.

mh2220-correspondence.connection: This completes the quotient spine: fibers, cosets, normality, induced maps and lattice correspondence express the same identification mechanism at different scales.

ureca-character-bound-kernel.hook: Can a character have maximum absolute value away from the kernel?
ureca-character-bound-kernel.objects: Fix a finite group G, a nonzero complex representation π:G→GL_d(C), and χ(g)=tr π(g). The representation is a left action on columns.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does χπ(1) measure?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The identity matrix has trace d, the dimension of the representation space.

examples.title: The central half-turn in the faithful D₈ plane action
steps: The square representation sends r² to −I₂.
Thus χ(r²)=−2 and |χ(r²)|=2=χ(1).
Yet r² is nonidentity and π(r²)≠I₂; it is not in the kernel.

examples.title: A non-scalar quarter-turn
steps: The real 90° rotation matrix has complex eigenvalues i and −i.
Its trace is zero, below the degree-two bound.
The two unit-circle phases cancel, so strict inequality detects a non-scalar image.

nonexample.title: Absolute trace as a kernel test
nonexample.explanation: The sign character of C₂ sends its nonidentity element to −1. Its trace has absolute value one, but its kernel is only the identity.

proofSteps: If g has order m, π(g)^m=I. Over C, x^m−1 has distinct roots, so π(g) diagonalizes with mth-root eigenvalues ζ₁,…,ζ_d.
Each |ζ_j|=1. The triangle inequality yields |Σζ_j|≤Σ|ζ_j|=d.
If Σζ_j=d, all real parts must equal one, hence every ζ_j=1 and π(g)=I.
If |Σζ_j|=d, equality in the triangle inequality makes all ζ_j share one phase λ, so π(g)=λI. The converse in each case is immediate.

boundaryCheck.question: Which trace condition characterizes membership in ker π?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The ordinary equality forces all finite-order eigenvalues to be 1. Absolute equality allows a nonidentity scalar such as −I.

application.question: For π(r²)=−I₂, what are χ(r²) and kernel membership?
choices: χ=−2; r² is not in the kernel
χ=2; r² is in the kernel
χ=−2; r² is in the kernel
application.explanation: The trace of −I₂ is −2; a kernel element must act as +I₂.

transfer.question: A degree-three finite-group representation has π(g)=ωI₃ with ω³=1 and ω≠1. What follows?
choices: |χ(g)|=3, yet g is not in the kernel
χ(g)=3 and g is in the kernel
transfer.explanation: χ(g)=3ω has absolute value 3, but 3ω≠3. This is a scalar preimage, not a kernel element.

ureca-character-bound-kernel.connection: Carry the scalar-equality distinction into the external tensor product: reciprocal nonidentity scalars can cancel.

ureca-external-tensor-products.hook: How can two different groups act on one tensor space?
ureca-external-tensor-products.objects: Let G,H be finite, π:G→GL(V), ρ:H→GL(W), and V,W nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector spaces. Product-group elements act on pure tensors.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which group acts in π⊠ρ?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The first group acts on V, the second on W, and a pair (g,h) acts on V⊗W.

examples.title: A C₃ character tensored with the D₈ plane
steps: Let a generate C₃ with π(a)=ω, and let ρ be the faithful two-dimensional D₈ square representation.
The product has degree 1·2=2; (a,r) acts by ωρ(r).
Since tr ρ(r)=0, the product character at (a,r) is ω·0=0.

examples.title: The cancellation preview
steps: Let the nontrivial C₂ element t act by −1 and D₈ central r² act by −I₂.
On a pure tensor, (t,r²) sends v⊗w to (−v)⊗(−w)=v⊗w.
Both factors act nontrivially on their own spaces, yet this pair acts trivially on V⊗W.

nonexample.title: Mixing tensor constructions
nonexample.explanation: The balancing relation (ur)⊗v=u⊗(rv) describes U⊗_R V for a right and left R-module. It is not the formula defining an action of G×H on a complex vector-space tensor product.

proofSteps: Define (g,h)·(v⊗w)=π(g)v⊗ρ(h)w and extend linearly; the tensor universal property makes this well-defined over C.
For (g₁,h₁)(g₂,h₂)=(g₁g₂,h₁h₂), composing operators gives π(g₁)π(g₂)⊗ρ(h₁)ρ(h₂), so the action law holds.
Inverse pairs act invertibly, and bases {v_i⊗w_j} show degree (dim V)(dim W).
The diagonal entries of A⊗B are A_ii B_jj. Summing i,j gives tr(A⊗B)=tr(A)tr(B).

boundaryCheck.question: What is needed to call this an external product of G and H representations?
choices: Both factors are representations over the same field and (g,h) acts by π(g)⊗ρ(h)
A right R-module and a left R-module alone
An action of G on both factors
boundaryCheck.explanation: The two representations share C here, and the acting group is G×H.

application.question: If χπ(a)=ω and χρ(r²)=−2, what is χπ⊠ρ(a,r²)?
application.explanation: Tensor-product traces multiply, giving ω·(−2).

transfer.question: What happens to the pair (t,r²) in sign(C₂)⊠square(D₈)?
choices: It acts as I on the tensor space
It is not a pair in C₂×D₈
transfer.explanation: The two negative scalar factors multiply to +1, so the pair is in the product kernel.

ureca-external-tensor-products.connection: Next factor inner products of these product characters to prove which external products are irreducible.

ureca-direct-product-irreducibles.hook: Could a direct product have an irreducible representation that is missing from the tensor list?
ureca-direct-product-irreducibles.objects: Let {π_i} and {ρ_j} be complete lists of finite-dimensional irreducible complex representations of finite G and H, with degrees d_i and e_j.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does character inner product 1 say for a genuine complex character?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: An actual complex character has self-inner-product equal to the sum of squared irreducible multiplicities; one forces one irreducible copy.

examples.title: All characters of C₂×C₃
steps: Each cyclic group has only degree-one complex irreducibles: two for C₂ and three for C₃.
Their six external products are pairwise distinct by factored orthogonality.
Six squared degrees sum to 6=|C₂×C₃|, so the six exhaust the irreducibles.

examples.title: Counting C₃×D₈
steps: D₈ has four degree-one irreducibles and one degree-two irreducible: 4·1²+2²=8.
C₃ has three degree-one irreducibles: 3·1²=3.
Their external products number 3·5=15; squared degrees sum 3·8=24=|C₃×D₈|.

nonexample.title: Counting candidates but skipping orthogonality
nonexample.explanation: Fifteen listed matrices need not be irreducible just because their squared dimensions sum to 24; first prove orthogonality and that each candidate is an actual representation.

proofSteps: Write χ_{i,j}(g,h)=χ_i(g)ψ_j(h). The inner-product sum over G×H separates into one sum over G and one over H.
Each factor inner product is Kronecker delta, so the product is δ_{ik}δ_{jℓ}. This proves the candidates are irreducible and pairwise inequivalent.
Compute Σ_{i,j}(d_i e_j)²=(Σ_i d_i²)(Σ_j e_j²)=|G||H|.
For finite groups over C, all irreducible squared degrees sum to the group order. The candidates use the whole total, so no further irreducible can occur.

boundaryCheck.question: Which combination proves the candidate list is complete?
choices: Factored orthogonality and a degree-squared total of |G||H|
Only a count of conjugacy classes of G
boundaryCheck.explanation: Orthogonality identifies distinct irreducibles; the full squared-degree total excludes an extra one.

application.question: How many irreducibles does C₃×D₈ have, and what is their squared-degree total?
application.explanation: Three C₃ characters pair with five D₈ irreducibles; 3(4·1²+1·2²)=24.

transfer.question: If G has irreducible degrees 1,1,2 and H has degrees 1,1,1, how many product irreducibles and what total squared degree?
transfer.explanation: There are 3·3=9 pairs; squared-degree sum is (1+1+4)(1+1+1)=18.

ureca-direct-product-irreducibles.connection: Now one can test faithfulness of each irreducible product using the actual scalar-preimage kernel rather than factor kernels alone.

ureca-product-kernel-scalar-matching.hook: How can two nonidentity operators multiply to the identity on a tensor product?
ureca-product-kernel-scalar-matching.objects: Representations π of G on V and ρ of H on W are finite-dimensional over C, with V,W nonzero. In the examples, D₈ square rotations act on columns.

prerequisiteCheck.question: If A⊗B is identity, what can A and B be?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A⊗B=I on nonzero finite-dimensional tensor factors forces A=λI and B=λ⁻¹I.

examples.title: Cancellation in C₂×D₈
steps: The faithful C₂ sign has π(t)=−1 and the faithful D₈ plane has ρ(r²)=−I₂.
The scalar pair is (−1,−1), whose product is +1.
Thus (t,r²) is a nonidentity product-kernel element although both individual kernels are trivial.

examples.title: No negative partner in C₃×D₈
steps: A faithful C₃ character takes values 1,ω,ω².
Only e and r² in the D₈ square representation act scalarly, by +1 and −1.
No nontrivial C₃ scalar is the reciprocal of −1; the product kernel is trivial.

nonexample.title: The product of factor kernels
nonexample.explanation: The two faithful representations above both have trivial kernels. Their Cartesian product contains only (e,e), missing (t,r²) in the external tensor kernel.

proofSteps: Let A⊗B=I and choose nonzero w. For every v, Av⊗Bw=v⊗w; uniqueness of pure-tensor factors forces Av=λ_v v and Bw=λ_v⁻¹w.
Since B and w are fixed, λ_v is constant for every nonzero v; linearity then gives A=λI and B=λ⁻¹I. Conversely reciprocal scalars tensor to I.
Apply this operator statement to A=π(g), B=ρ(h) to obtain the exact kernel set.
If π is faithful and π(g) is scalar, it commutes with every π(x); faithfulness forces g to commute with every x, so g∈Z(G). Repeat for H. This center conclusion needs faithfulness.

boundaryCheck.question: When can scalar preimages be restricted to group centers by this argument?
choices: For every representation regardless of kernel
Only if both groups are abelian
boundaryCheck.explanation: A scalar image makes the represented commutator trivial. Faithfulness is needed to conclude the group commutator itself is trivial.

application.question: Which nonidentity pair is in sign(C₂)⊠square(D₈) kernel?
application.explanation: Both factors of (t,r²) act as −I, so their tensor is identity.

transfer.question: Why is faithful(C₃)⊠faithful(D₈ square) faithful?
choices: Both factors are faithful, which alone is sufficient
transfer.explanation: The reciprocal scalar sets intersect only at 1. Faithful factors alone do not suffice, as C₂×D₈ shows.

ureca-product-kernel-scalar-matching.connection: Schur turns these scalar preimages into central characters; compare their root-of-unity images to decide whether a product is faithful.

ureca-faithful-direct-product.hook: Exactly when can faithful irreducibles of two groups combine faithfully?
ureca-faithful-direct-product.objects: G,H are finite; all representations are nonzero, finite-dimensional and complex. D₈ means the order-eight square group, not a sixteen-element convention.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does Schur imply for a central element in a complex irreducible?
choices: It need not commute with the representation
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A central element yields an intertwiner; over C, Schur makes it scalar.

examples.title: C₂×D₈ fails
steps: The sign of C₂ is faithful and the geometric D₈ plane is faithful irreducible.
Their center orders are 2 and 2; the common scalar −1 gives (t,r²) in the tensor kernel.
Every irreducible of C₂×D₈ is a product, so no alternative faithful irreducible escapes this obstruction.

examples.title: C₃×D₈ succeeds
steps: Use the faithful C₃ character a↦ω and the faithful D₈ square plane.
Their centers have orders 3 and 2, hence common scalar image only {1}.
The external product is irreducible by character inner-product factorisation and faithful by scalar matching.

nonexample.title: Cyclic center as a complete test
nonexample.explanation: A faithful irreducible forces an injective center character, hence cyclic center. The converse is not asserted for an arbitrary finite group; the direct-product criterion also assumes each factor has a faithful irreducible.

proofSteps: For faithful irreducible π, Schur gives π(z)=α(z)I for z∈Z(G). Faithfulness makes α injective; similarly β for H.
Finite subgroups of C× are cyclic. The images are μ_a and μ_b, where a=|Z(G)| and b=|Z(H)|. Their intersection has gcd(a,b) elements.
Each common scalar gives exactly one central pair with α(z)β(w)=1, so |ker(π⊠ρ)|=gcd(a,b). Thus coprime centers and faithful factors suffice.

Conversely, a faithful irreducible of G×H is π⊠ρ by the previous lesson. If either factor had a kernel, its product with identity would lie in the product kernel. Both factors are faithful, and the same gcd formula forces coprime center orders.

boundaryCheck.question: Which package of conditions makes the coprime-center criterion valid?
choices: Finite groups, complex irreducibles, and each factor has a faithful irreducible
Finite groups over any field without further hypotheses
boundaryCheck.explanation: The proof uses complex Schur, finite scalar images and faithful irreducible factors. Coprime centers alone do not create missing factor representations.

application.question: What is the kernel size for faithful irreducible factors with center orders 6 and 4?
application.explanation: The common root-of-unity subgroup has order gcd(6,4)=2.

transfer.question: Which product admits a faithful irreducible with D₈: C₂×D₈ or C₃×D₈?
choices: Both, because each factor is faithful
transfer.explanation: D₈ has a faithful irreducible with center order 2. The C₃ center order is coprime to 2; the C₂ order is not.

ureca-faithful-direct-product.connection: The representation route now joins Maschke, Schur, character inner products, tables, external products and the scalar-compatibility capstone.

mh2220-burnside.hook: A rotation moves every vertex. Can it still fix a coloring?
mh2220-burnside.objects: Let a finite group G act on a finite position set P on the left. It acts on colorings c:P→{red,blue} by (g·c)(p)=c(g⁻¹p). A fixed coloring is constant on every cycle of the position permutation; unused colors are allowed.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For a left action, what is the stabilizer of a coloring c?
choices: All elements that fix one chosen vertex
The set of colors used by c
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A stabilizer consists of all group elements fixing the whole coloring, not just one position.

examples.title: Three rotations of a binary triangle
steps: The identity has three one-cycles on positions and fixes 2³=8 colorings.
Each nonidentity rotation has one three-cycle, fixes no position, but fixes two constant colorings.
The fixed-coloring table is 8,2,2. Average (8+2+2)/3=4 orbits.

examples.title: Four beads under quarter-turns
steps: The rotations by 0,1,2,3 steps have 4,1,2,1 cycles.
With two labeled colors their fixed-coloring counts are 16,2,4,2.
The average is 24/4=6 necklaces, not 16/4=4.

nonexample.title: Divide total colorings by group order
nonexample.explanation: On the triangle, 8/3 is not even an integer. The two constant colorings each have the whole rotation group as stabilizer, so the coloring action is not free.

proofSteps: Count pairs (g,c) for which g·c=c, first by g. This yields the sum of all fixed-coloring counts.
Count the same pairs by c. A coloring contributes the size of its stabilizer.
Within one coloring orbit, orbit–stabilizer gives orbit size times stabilizer size equal to |G|. Every orbit therefore contributes |G| pairs. Divide by |G|.

boundaryCheck.question: A triangle rotation fixes no vertex. How many binary colorings can it fix?
choices: Zero, because it fixes no vertex
Two, because its single three-cycle can have either color
Six, because it moves three vertices
boundaryCheck.explanation: Fixed positions and fixed colorings differ: every cycle must be monochromatic, yielding two constant colorings.

application.question: The four rotations of a square fix 16,2,4,2 binary colorings. How many orbits?
application.explanation: The fixed counts sum to 24; averaging over four rotations gives six orbits.

transfer.question: A permutation of five positions has cycles of lengths 2 and 3. With three labeled colors, how many colorings does it fix?
transfer.explanation: One color may be chosen independently for each of the two cycles, giving 3²=9 fixed colorings.

mh2220-burnside.connection: Necklace and cube counts use the same double count. Their only new work is to derive the position-cycle table accurately.

mh2220-necklaces.hook: Why do six binary beads give fourteen necklaces but thirteen bracelets?
mh2220-necklaces.objects: Number n bead positions 0,…,n−1 around a polygon. Cₙ has n rotations; Dₙ has those rotations plus n reflections. A necklace identifies rotations only; a bracelet also identifies reflections. Colors are labeled, may repeat, and need not all appear.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which group acts when mirror images are also identified?
choices: The group of all color permutations
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Adding reflections to the rotations forms the dihedral action of order 2n.

examples.title: Six beads: all rotation rows
steps: Rotation by k steps has gcd(6,k) cycles. For k=0,1,2,3,4,5 the cycle counts are 6,1,2,3,2,1.
Binary fixed-coloring counts are 64,2,4,8,4,2, summing to 84.
Averaging the six rotations gives 14 necklaces. The two monochromatic colorings remain included.

examples.title: Six beads: two reflection types
steps: Three axes pass through opposite beads. Each fixes two beads and swaps the other four in two pairs: 1²2², four cycles, 2⁴=16 fixed colorings.
Three axes pass through opposite gaps. Each swaps three pairs: 2³, three cycles, 2³=8 fixed colorings.
The dihedral total is 84+3·16+3·8=156. Divide by 12 to get 13 bracelets.

nonexample.title: Treat all even reflections alike
nonexample.explanation: For n even, an axis through opposite beads fixes two positions; an axis through gaps fixes none. At n=6 they have four versus three cycles, hence 16 versus 8 fixed binary colorings.

proofSteps: For a rotation by k steps, the orbit of position 0 has length n/gcd(n,k), and there are gcd(n,k) disjoint cycles. It fixes q^gcd(n,k) colorings.
For odd n, each reflection fixes one bead and pairs the rest, giving (n+1)/2 cycles.
For even n, n/2 axes through opposite beads have n/2+1 cycles, while n/2 gap axes have n/2 cycles. Average all rotation and reflection fixed-coloring counts over 2n elements.

boundaryCheck.question: Which statement about even-n reflections is correct?
choices: Half have two fixed beads and half have none
boundaryCheck.explanation: Even polygons have two geometric axis types; their fixed-position and cycle counts differ.

application.question: For six binary beads, how many bracelets result from the rotation sum 84 and reflection contributions 3·16+3·8?
application.explanation: The full sum is 156 and |D₆|=12, so the result is 13.

transfer.question: For five beads and q colors, how many colorings does one reflection fix?
transfer.explanation: An odd-polygon reflection fixes one bead and pairs the other four, giving three cycles and q³ fixed colorings.

mh2220-necklaces.connection: The cycle index records all these cycle lengths. It can count a chosen color inventory, not just any assignment from q colors.

mh2220-cycle-index.hook: How can a fixed-point table count colorings with exactly two red beads?
mh2220-cycle-index.objects: For a finite group G on n positions, cⱼ(g) is the number of j-cycles of g, including fixed points as one-cycles. Define Z_G(a₁,…,aₙ)=|G|⁻¹Σ_g∏ⱼ aⱼ^cⱼ(g). For two labeled colors red and blue, substitute aⱼ=xʲ+yʲ.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does a one-cycle in a position permutation represent?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A position fixed by one group element is a cycle of length one and contributes its own color choice.

examples.title: Triangle rotations: derive the polynomial
steps: The identity has cycle type 1³; the two nonidentity rotations each have type 3¹. Thus Z=(a₁³+2a₃)/3.
Replace a₁ with x+y and a₃ with x³+y³. Expand to ((x+y)³+2(x³+y³))/3.
The result is x³+x²y+xy²+y³. The coefficient of x²y is 1: one orbit has exactly two red beads.

examples.title: Four-bead rotation inventory
steps: The four cycle types are 1⁴, 4, 2², 4, so Z=(a₁⁴+a₂²+2a₄)/4.
For exactly two red beads, the identity contributes coefficient 6 in (x+y)⁴, the half-turn contributes coefficient 2 in (x²+y²)², and quarter-turns contribute 0.
The coefficient after averaging is (6+2)/4=2 rotational orbits with two red beads.

nonexample.title: Substitute aⱼ=2 and expect an inventory
nonexample.explanation: Setting every aⱼ=2 gives the total number of binary coloring orbits, with all inventories mixed. It cannot say how many have exactly two red beads; the variables x and y must retain color multiplicities.

proofSteps: A coloring fixed by g is constant on each cycle. A j-cycle contributes either xʲ or yʲ to the weighted color inventory.
Multiply (xʲ+yʲ) over every cycle of g. The coefficient of xʳyⁿ⁻ʳ counts fixed colorings with exactly r red beads.
Average these weighted fixed-coloring polynomials over G. Burnside applies to each invariant inventory separately, so the coefficient in Z after substitution counts its orbits.

For the full symmetric group Sᵣ on r positions and q labelled colors, a permutation σ fixes q^c(σ) colorings because each cycle has one freely chosen color. Burnside therefore gives r!⁻¹Σσq^c(σ) orbits.
Two colorings are in the same Sᵣ-orbit exactly when their q color counts agree: a permutation matches the positions of each color. Thus orbits correspond to nonnegative counts summing to r.
For q≥1, encode those counts by r identical marks and q−1 separators. Choosing the mark positions in a string of length r+q−1 gives binomial(q+r−1,r), including r=0.

Multiplying the orbit identity by r! gives Σσq^c(σ)=q(q+1)⋯(q+r−1). Both sides are polynomials in q of degree at most r and agree at every positive integer. Their difference has infinitely many roots, so it is the zero polynomial; replace q by x.

boundaryCheck.question: Which substitution retains exactly how many red beads are used?
boundaryCheck.explanation: A j-cycle uses j beads of one color, so its monomial must carry exponent j.

application.question: The triangle cycle index is (a₁³+2a₃)/3. What is the coefficient of x²y after aⱼ=xʲ+yʲ?
application.explanation: Only (x+y)³ supplies x²y, with coefficient 3; divide by 3 to obtain one orbit.

transfer.question: For four beads under rotations, identity contributes 6 and half-turn contributes 2 fixed colorings with exactly two red beads; quarter-turns contribute 0. How many orbits have that inventory?
transfer.explanation: Burnside coefficient by coefficient gives (6+2+0+0)/4=2.

mh2220-cycle-index.connection: The same cycle-index calculation works for cube vertices, faces and edges once their different cycle tables are derived from the rotations.

mh2220-solid-colorings.hook: Why do the same twenty-four cube rotations give different coloring polynomials on vertices, faces and edges?
mh2220-solid-colorings.objects: Use the 24 orientation-preserving signed-permutation matrices of the centered cube. They act separately on eight vertices, six face centers and twelve edge midpoints. Color these labeled positions with q labeled colors; repetition and unused colors are allowed. Only proper rotations are averaged.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What must be known before applying Burnside to cube-vertex colorings?
choices: The cycle decomposition on vertices of every rotation class
The number of visible faces in a drawing
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The fixed-coloring count is q to the number of vertex cycles, so the action on the chosen feature set matters.

examples.title: All five cube rotation-axis families on vertices
steps: Identity: one element, cycle type 1⁸, contribution q⁸. Six face-axis quarter-turns each have type 4², contributing 6q².
Three face-axis half-turns and six edge-axis half-turns each have type 2⁴, contributing 9q⁴. Eight vertex-axis third-turns each have type 1²3², contributing 8q⁴.
The family counts 1+6+3+8+6=24. Sum q⁸+17q⁴+6q²; divide by 24. At q=2 the answer is 23.

examples.title: One motion, two feature sets
steps: A 90° face-axis rotation acts on eight vertices in two four-cycles, so it fixes q² vertex colorings and no individual vertex.
On six faces it fixes the two axis faces and cycles the other four, type 1²4, so it fixes q³ face colorings.
The group element is unchanged; only the chosen action set differs. The lab shows vertices, faces and edges separately.

nonexample.title: Use a vertex polynomial to count face colorings
nonexample.explanation: The axis faces remain fixed under a face-axis quarter-turn, but no vertex does. Thus its face and vertex cycle counts differ. The displayed vertex polynomial cannot be reused for faces or edges.

proofSteps: Classify each proper rotation by axis and angle: identity; six face quarter-turns; three face half-turns; eight vertex third-turns; six edge half-turns.
Apply each representative matrix to the selected feature set, compute its disjoint cycles, and raise q to the number of cycles. The table verifies every member of each family.
Sum class size times fixed-coloring count and divide by 24. This is Burnside for the chosen finite rotation action; switching feature sets requires a new cycle ledger.

boundaryCheck.question: A face-axis quarter-turn on the cube has which vertex and face cycle counts?
choices: Two vertex cycles and three face cycles
Three vertex cycles and two face cycles
Eight vertex cycles and six face cycles
boundaryCheck.explanation: The vertices split into two four-cycles; the two axis faces are fixed and the other four faces make a four-cycle.

application.question: For q=2, what does (q⁸+17q⁴+6q²)/24 give?
application.explanation: (256+272+24)/24=552/24=23 rotation orbits of binary vertex colorings.

transfer.question: A cube face-axis quarter-turn has face cycle type 1²4. With three labeled colors, how many face colorings does it fix?
transfer.explanation: The two fixed faces and one four-cycle are three independent cycles, so there are 3³ choices.

mh2220-solid-colorings.connection: The same geometric rotations induce different permutation representations on vertices, faces and edges. This distinction recurs when constructing characters from fixed points.

orthogonal-metric-orientation.hook: A plane reflection and central inversion both reverse orientation in R³. Do they fix the same vectors?
orthogonal-metric-orientation.objects: Real column vectors with the usual dot product. Q is orthogonal when QᵀQ=I. A plane reflection Hₙ=I−2nnᵀ uses a unit normal n in R³; −I₃ is central inversion, not a plane reflection.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the dot product of u=(1,2) and v=(0,1)?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Multiply matching coordinates and add: 1·0+2·1=2.

examples.title: One matrix preserves every inner product
steps: For F=diag(1,−1), FᵀF=I₂ and det F=−1.
With u=(1,2), v=(0,1), their images are Fu=(1,−2), Fv=(0,−1). Both dot products equal 2.
F fixes (x,0) and reverses the perpendicular y-direction.

examples.title: Same determinant, different fixed spaces
steps: For unit n=(1,0,0), Hₙ=diag(−1,1,1), det Hₙ=−1, and the fixed plane is x=0.
Central inversion −I₃ has determinant (−1)³=−1, but −v=v over R forces v=0.
Both maps preserve inner products and cube vertices, yet one fixes a plane and the other only the origin.

nonexample.title: A metric map need not preserve a chosen solid
nonexample.explanation: Rotate R³ by 37° around the z-axis. It is orthogonal with determinant +1, but a cube vertex generally leaves the vertex set. The cube-preservation condition is extra.

proofSteps: From QᵀQ=I, (Qu)ᵀ(Qv)=uᵀQᵀQv=uᵀv for all real column vectors u,v; lengths and angles follow.
Taking determinants gives (det Q)²=1, hence det Q is +1 or −1.
For unit n, Hₙn=−n, while Hₙv=v for every v perpendicular to n. An orthonormal basis beginning with n gives determinant −1 and fixed-space dimension two in R³.
For −I₃, every direction has eigenvalue −1, so determinant −1 and fixed-space dimension zero. Determinant alone does not identify a reflection plane.

boundaryCheck.question: Which claim follows from QᵀQ=I for a real 3×3 matrix?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The matrix identity gives metric preservation. Determinant may be −1, and an arbitrary orthogonal map need not preserve a particular finite solid.

application.question: For H=diag(−1,1,1), what is its fixed space?
application.explanation: H(x,y,z)=(−x,y,z), so H v=v exactly when x=0.

transfer.question: A real 3×3 orthogonal Q has determinant −1 and fixes no nonzero vector. Which displayed example has that property?
transfer.explanation: −I₃ fixes only zero. The plane reflection fixes a two-dimensional plane; the R² matrix has a different dimension.

orthogonal-metric-orientation.connection: The next lesson fixes the plane reflection F=diag(1,−1) and compares the order of composition with rotations.

orthogonal-plane.hook: Reflect, then turn; turn, then reflect. Why do the mirror lines separate?
orthogonal-plane.objects: Real plane column vectors. Rθ rotates counterclockwise through θ. F=diag(1,−1) reflects across the x-axis. Products act right factor first, so RθF and FRθ use the same F in opposite orders.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does F=diag(1,−1) do to (2,3)?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: F keeps the first coordinate and negates the second, so its fixed line is the x-axis.

examples.title: The zero-angle gate
steps: At θ=0, R₀=I₂. Therefore R₀F=FR₀=F=diag(1,−1).
Both products fix the x-axis, and both send (1,0) to itself. The drawn line and matrix must agree.

examples.title: A quarter-turn separates the lines
steps: At θ=90°, RθF has matrix [[0,1],[1,0]], whose fixed line is y=x, at +45°.
FRθ has matrix [[0,−1],[−1,0]], whose fixed line is y=−x, at −45°.
Their matrices and fixed lines differ even though both have determinant −1.

nonexample.title: The angle is not the mirror-line angle
